rows.why: The rows that settle an open question are 2d and 250ms, which depend on which units are accepted. Item 2 accepts d and ms, which gives 172800000 and 250. Item 10 also bears on the 0s and 1d0h0m0s0ms rows, and its pick accepts those too.
Item 7 asks how whitespace is handled. Its pick trims whitespace around the whole string, so '  45m\n' parses to 2700000.

This scenario covers many items (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10). Most picks match it, but item 10 is the one where they differ. S3 expects '05s' to be rejected, while item 10 accepts leading zeros (it turns '007s' into 7000).
No item asks whether one component's count may exceed the next larger unit, as in 90m. Item 4 covers order and repeated units, not how big a single count can be.
Item 4 asks about component order and repeated units. Its pick requires strictly descending units with no repeats, which rejects 30m1h, 1h1h, 1s500ms2s and 5ms1s.
Item 9 sets the upper bound at 2^53-1 ms. The input adds up to exactly 9007199254740991, so it is inside the bound and parses.
Item 9's pick returns an error above 9007199254740991 and checks both while reading digits and when multiplying by the unit. That covers the sum that is one too big and the 20-digit count.
Item 11's pick prints a greedy largest-first breakdown into d/h/m/s/ms, skips zero components and prints 0ms for zero. That produces every expected string.
Item 11's pick never goes above days and skips zero components, so 2^53-1 prints as 104249991d8h59m991ms, with the zero seconds left out.
No item asks whether formatting and then parsing gives the number back. That follows from other choices but is not one of the listed questions.

Item 12 asks what formatting does with negative or too-large values. Its pick returns "" and an error below 0 or above 2^53-1, which covers all four values. The pick doesn't give the error text, so it doesn't confirm the word 'milliseconds'.
